bp: Online news and social platforms show people far more headlines than they can carefully inspect. A headline has one job for the reader: summarize enough of the story that the reader can decide whether opening it is worth attention. Clickbait bends that job. It uses exaggeration, missing context, or emotional promise to win the click before the reader has evidence. This paper serves the practical system that must decide whether a news title is honestly informative or mainly trying to pull attention. The difficulty is sharper because modern language models can write explanations that sound helpful, but they may also flatter the viewpoint implied by the prompt. The paper calls that tendency sycophancy: the model gives reasoning that matches a user's stance instead of a truth-seeking instruction. Rather than only treating that as a defect, the work asks whether the defect can be turned into useful opposing arguments for clickbait detection.
wh: The hard part is that clickbait is not a fixed list of suspicious words. A headline can be short, emotional, incomplete, or surprising without being deceptive. Another headline can look calm while still overpromising what the article supports. A simple detector that memorizes surface cues will mistake style for intent. Large language models seem attractive because they can explain why a headline looks credible or deceptive, but the abstract says their reasoning is hindered by sycophancy. If asked in a way that hints at a belief, the model may produce a pleasing argument for that belief rather than a balanced judgment. That creates a second failure: the explanation itself becomes biased evidence. The paper's tension is therefore unusual. It needs reasoning about the headline, but it cannot blindly trust a single model explanation. It needs disagreement, but useful disagreement must be generated without known labels for every title.
naive: A smart beginner might ask a large language model, "Is this headline clickbait? Explain your answer," then use the answer as the detector. That fails when the model follows the user's implied stance or prompt wording instead of testing the headline. Another beginner might fine-tune a smaller text classifier on labeled clickbait examples. That can work when future titles resemble the training data, but it may learn cheap cues such as emotional phrasing or question marks, and it needs labels. A third attempt is to ask for one credibility score. The abstract suggests this is too thin: a single score hides the reasons on both sides and gives the local detector little structure to learn from.
ap: The central move is to make the language model argue from both sides on purpose. For each news title, the Self-renewal Opposing-stance Reasoning Generation method prompts the model to produce an "agree" line of reasoning and a "disagree" line of reasoning. In plain terms, it asks the model to act as two readers: one who can explain why the title may be deceptive and one who can explain why it may be acceptable. This uses the model's stance-following habit as a generator of paired evidence, not as the final judge. Then a local clickbait detector, called ORCD, learns from the title together with these two arguments. The paper uses three BERT encoders, meaning three smaller text readers trained to turn the title and each reasoning text into comparable internal descriptions. Soft credibility scores from the language model guide learning without requiring ordinary ground-truth labels for generating the reasoning pairs.
mech: The mechanism starts with one object: a news title whose clickbait status is unknown or expensive to label. First, the SORG process asks a large language model to renew or generate reasoning from opposing stances. One generated text supports the idea that the title should be treated as clickbait or low-credibility; the other supports the opposite view. The important output of this stage is not a final yes-or-no answer. It is a pair of explanations that expose the tension in the title. Second, the system obtains language-model credibility scores, which become soft labels. A soft label is not a hard sticker saying "true" or "false"; it is a graded training signal saying how strongly the generated evidence points in a direction. Third, ORCD feeds three pieces of text through three BERT encoders: the title, the agreeing reasoning, and the disagreeing reasoning. Each encoder produces a compact numerical description of its text. The detector then compares these descriptions so that the title representation is interpreted through both supporting and opposing arguments. Training uses contrastive learning, which means examples or views that should agree are pulled closer in the model's comparison space, while views that should not be confused are pushed apart. The final output is a local detector that classifies clickbait without prompting a large model at inference time for the whole decision.
math: The math is mainly about comparison under uncertain supervision. The first object is a pair: two reasoned views of the same headline from opposite stances. Pairing matters because a single explanation can drift with the prompt, while a pair creates a structured difference the model can measure. The second object is a learned description, often called an embedding; here that means a list of numbers used as a compact handle for a title or reasoning text. These number lists are useful only if nearness has the right meaning: the title should be near the reasoning that genuinely explains its clickbait signal and farther from reasoning that should not drive the same judgment. Contrastive learning is the rule for shaping that space. It teaches by relative comparison instead of only by independent labels: this view should align with that view, and this other view should be separated. The third idea is soft labeling. Instead of pretending an automatically generated credibility score is certain, the score gives a graded amount of trust. The tradeoff is signal versus noise. The method gains many training cues without human labels for every generated argument, but those cues inherit uncertainty from the language model that produced them.
dots: This paper connects directly to the repository's misinformation and trust family: it treats clickbait as a broken trust chain, where a fluent headline must be checked against evidence about how it persuades. It also connects to the language-model family, because the paper is not satisfied with a fluent answer from a large model. It builds control around that model by forcing opposed stances and handing the result to a smaller local detector. The similarity concept also appears: the detector learns which title-and-reasoning descriptions should sit near each other for a trustworthy decision. Probability appears through soft credibility scores, because the training signal is a degree of belief rather than a clean fact. Neighboring papers in the same batch include FakeAgent for misinformation in micro-videos and PAMAS for multi-agent misinformation detection. They differ in surface material, but share the deeper pressure: one weak clue is not enough, so the system gathers several perspectives and combines them carefully.
ww: The method should improve over the naive approach because it removes the single-explanation bottleneck. If a large model is asked for one answer, sycophancy can make the answer follow the prompt's implied belief. If the same tendency is used deliberately to generate both an agreeing and a disagreeing argument, the detector can inspect the contrast between them. That contrast is useful because clickbait detection often depends on what is missing, exaggerated, or overclaimed, not just on the headline's words. Opposing reasoning can make those hidden alternatives visible: why someone might be tempted to click, and why the title may or may not deserve that attention. The local ORCD model then learns stable patterns across many such pairs. The three-reader design keeps the title and the two explanations distinct before combining them, so one stance does not immediately overwrite the other. Soft scores help because generated reasoning is not treated as perfect truth; it is treated as graded evidence that can guide separation while leaving room for uncertainty.
po: The payoff is a clickbait detector that uses large-model reasoning without relying on one large-model prompt as the final decision. According to the abstract, SORG can generate high-quality agree and disagree reasoning pairs for a title without requiring ground-truth labels, and ORCD uses those pairs with soft credibility guidance. The reported evaluation on three benchmark datasets says the method consistently outperforms direct large-model prompting, fine-tuned smaller language models, and prior clickbait detection methods. In practical terms, the system buys a way to turn an unreliable stance-following habit into training material for a more focused detector.
limits: Several assumptions must hold. The generated agree and disagree arguments must contain real cues about clickbait, not just polished rationalizations. The language-model credibility scores must be informative enough for soft labels, even though the same model family can be sycophantic. The three BERT encoders must learn distinctions that transfer beyond the three evaluated datasets. The abstract does not prove performance on new platforms, languages, coordinated headline farms, or cases where the article body is needed to judge exaggeration. It also does not show that the generated reasoning is truthful; it shows that it can be useful for detection under the reported setup.
